title: Mitigation of harmful algal bloom (Margalefidinium polykrikoides) intensity and toxicity via aeration processes
scale: lab flasks: 150 mL (shaking) or 500 mL cultures in 1 L Erlenmeyer flasks; field bloom water 500 mL flasks in a flow-through outdoor table
dose: macrobubbles via air stone at 25 mL/min (low) or 300 mL/min (high), continuous; nanobubbles (~100 nm) generated 2 h in 500 L (Moleaer XTB 200), ± ozone; orbital shaking 240 rpm (est. epsilon ~8 x 10^-2 m2 s-3)
duration: lab ~10-15 d; bloom-water experiments 24 h (Old Fort Pond) and 2 d (Meetinghouse Creek)
result: High-rate macrobubbles cut M. polykrikoides 21-58% (CPSB-1G) and 34-63% (CP1) vs unaerated controls, and 78% at day 10 in the screening test; high-level treatment gave 0% larval fish mortality vs 100% in controls within 1.5 h. In bloom water, cells were 1477 vs 2022 cells/mL in controls after 24 h (Old Fort Pond) and 29-55% in 2 d (Meetinghouse Creek).
env_effects: In Meetinghouse Creek bloom water, Polykrikos sp. and Prorocentrum cordatum increased under macrobubbling while M. polykrikoides fell.
key_details: Screening test (strain CPSB-1G, 4 replicates, 500 cells/mL) compared orbital shaking at 240 rpm, nanobubbles with and without ozone, and macrobubbles at 300 mL/min; by day 10 macrobubbles were 78% below control and 72% below both nanobubble treatments. In two-level tests (25 vs 300 mL/min, n=4), high-rate bubbling cut CPSB-1G 21-58% and CP1 34-63% vs unaerated controls; Fv/Fm dropped under both rates. Larval M. beryllina had 0% mortality in high-level bubbling vs 100% in the positive control within 1.5 h; C. variegatus survival was 100% under both bubbling rates. In bloom water (n=3), Old Fort Pond cells went from 2000 to 1477 +/- 94 (high) vs 2022 +/- 14 (control) cells/mL in 24 h; at Meetinghouse Creek, M. polykrikoides fell 55% (low) and 29% (high) by day 2. Orbital shaking also significantly reduced growth (days 6-12). Caveat: small flasks with bubbling fitted to 0.5 L volumes; no scale-up tested.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record's '>60%' is from the highlights; the reported ranges are 21-58% (CPSB-1G) and 34-63% (CP1) for high-level bubbling, 78% at day 10 in screening. Flow rates (25 and 300 mL/min) and durations are given. The field arm was bloom water in flasks, not in-situ aeration. In one bloom test the low rate beat the high rate (55% vs 29%).

title: Quantified small-scale turbulence inhibits a red tide dinoflagellate, Gonyaulax polyedra Stein
venue: Deep Sea Research Part A. Oceanographic Research Papers
scale: Couette cylinders
dose: constant shear rate γ
result: Zero growth at γ ≈ 8 s⁻¹, negative growth above 8, no effect below 2 s⁻¹ (via Gibson & Thomas 1995).

title: Effects of turbulence intermittency on growth inhibition of a red tide dinoflagellate, Gonyaulax polyedra Stein
scale: Couette
dose: γ ≈ 9 s⁻¹ for 5 min to 2.5 h per day
result: 0.25-2.5 h/day gave negative growth; 5 min/day had no effect; the daily-mean γ needed for zero growth fell to <0.09 s⁻¹ with intermittency.

title: EFFECTS OF SMALL‐SCALE TURBULENCE ON PHOTOSYNTHESIS, PIGMENTATION, CELL DIVISION, AND CELL SIZE IN THE MARINE DINOFLAGELLATE GOMAULAX POLYEDRA (DINOPHYCEAE) 1
scale: rotating bottles + Couette
dose: up to 26.6 s⁻¹
result: Photosynthesis was less sensitive than growth; photosynthesis per cell and respiration rose.

title: EFFECTS OF TURBULENCE ON THE MARINE DINOFLAGELLATE GYMNODINIUM NELSONII 1
scale: flasks, orbital shaker 100 rpm
dose: shaking at 100 rpm
result: Division stopped, cell volume up to 1.5× and DNA/RNA per cell up to 10×; after a 10-day shake division resumed at ~2/3 the control rate; >20 d gave total death.

title: Species‐specific physiological response of dinoflagellates to quantified small‐scale turbulence 1
organism: Alexandrium minutum, Prorocentrum triestinum, Gymnodinium sp.
scale: flasks, orbital shaker 100 rpm
dose: ε ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁴ m² s⁻³
result: Shaking cut net growth rate to 33% of still controls in A. minutum (0.108 vs 0.328 d⁻¹) and to 28% in P. triestinum (0.136 vs 0.485 d⁻¹), i.e. roughly two-thirds lower; small Gymnodinium sp. was not significantly affected. Cell volume rose up to 1.4x/2.5x and DNA per cell 1.8x/5.3x; swimming speed halved; cells recovered in still water.
key_details: Lab flask experiments at 20°C, orbital shaker at 100 rpm (bulk ε ≈ 2 cm² s⁻³, measured by acoustic Doppler velocimeter), comparing still controls with flasks shaken during exponential growth, then returned to still conditions. Replication was two flasks per treatment once shaking began (six before). Table 3 gives turbulent/still growth ratios (T/S) of 33% (A. minutum, p = 0.009) and 28% (P. triestinum, p = 0.003); after shaking stopped, growth recovered to 62% and 46% of control rates. Gymnodinium sp. T/S was 79-99%, not significant. Response was species-specific with no clear link to taxonomy or morphology; shaker turbulence is far above typical ocean levels.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record reads the abstract's '33% and 28%' as reductions; Table 3 shows these are turbulent/still growth-rate ratios, so growth was reduced by about 67% and 72%.

title: CELL CYCLE AND CELL MORTALITY OF ALEXANDRIUM MINUTUM (DINOPHYCEAE) UNDER SMALL‐SCALE TURBULENCE CONDITIONS 1
scale: 4 flasks: 2 shaken (orbital shaker, 120 rpm, 30 mm displacement) vs 2 still controls
dose: ε = 27 cm² s⁻³ (2.7 × 10⁻³ W kg⁻¹), orbital shaker
duration: Continuous shaking from day 7 to day 21 (~14 d)
result: Shaken cultures grew at 0.52 ± 0.06 d⁻¹ vs 0.69 ± 0.11 d⁻¹ still (75% of control); final abundance (days 16-21) 27,852 vs 54,333 cells mL⁻¹ (~51% of still). Immediate transient G2/M arrest; mortality signals only after >4 d.
key_details: Synchronised A. minutum cultures; on day 7 two flasks were randomly shaken and two kept still (n = 2 flasks per treatment). Turbulence came from an orbital shaker at 120 rpm, ε = 27 cm² s⁻³. Shaken exponential growth rate was 0.52 ± 0.06 d⁻¹ vs 0.69 ± 0.11 d⁻¹ in still cultures (P = 0.005), and final cell abundance was ~51% of the still cultures (27,852 ± 3,461 vs 54,333 ± 14,917 cells mL⁻¹). After 48 h of shaking, G2/M lasted ~75% longer and S phase was ~19% shorter. Mortality was estimated only qualitatively (Coulter size fractions of broken thecae); the authors state no rates could be estimated.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record gave ε ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁴; the paper states ε = 27 cm² s⁻³ = 2.7 × 10⁻³ W kg⁻¹. The record also left out the growth and abundance reductions (75% of the still growth rate; ~51% of final cells).

title: Modulation of ecdysal cyst and toxin dynamics of two Alexandrium (Dinophyceae) species under small-scale turbulence
scale: Culture flasks, n = 2 per treatment; orbital shaker (high ε) and orbital grid system (low ε), 5 experiments
duration: Shaking for 4 d (exponential or stationary phase) or continuously ('Always', ~16-17 d, days 4/5 to 21)
result: At high ε, continuously shaken A. minutum grew at 0.19 ± 0.02 vs 0.25 ± 0.01 d⁻¹ and ended at 55.4% of control cell numbers; A. catenella ended at 24.7% and 21.6% of control (two experiments). Low ε (grids) did not suppress growth (A. minutum 127% of control).
env_effects: Ecdysal cyst production was inhibited during shaking and recovered when shaking stopped. Cellular GTX(1+4) toxin was lower under long shaking, e.g. A. catenella 109.2 vs 169.7 fmol cell⁻¹.
key_details: Two Alexandrium species were exposed to ε = 0.4 cm² s⁻³ (orbital grids) or 27 cm² s⁻³ (orbital shaker), for 4 d in exponential or stationary phase or continuously, against still controls (n = 2 flasks per treatment). Continuous shaking at high ε cut A. minutum growth from 0.25 to 0.19 d⁻¹ and final abundance to 55.4% of control (4,690 vs 8,458 cells mL⁻¹). A. catenella final abundance was 24.7% and 21.6% of control, with growth rate not markedly changed. Four-day shaking gave only 86.5-96.3% of control abundance. Low-ε grids favoured growth (A. minutum 127% of control), with cells escaping to calmer layers.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record reads the abstract's 'ca. 55.4%' and 'ca. 23%' as reductions. Table 1 shows them as the share of control that remained (%T/S): A. minutum was ~45% lower and A. catenella ~75-78% lower (24.7%/21.6% of control). The record understates the A. catenella effect by a factor of about 3.

title: EFFECTS OF SMALL‐SCALE TURBULENCE ON NET GROWTH RATE AND SIZE OF TEN SPECIES OF MARINE DINOFLAGELLATES 1
scale: 20 L polycarbonate tanks (24 x 10 x 100 cm, filled to 80 cm), turbulence from a pair of vertically oscillating 2.5 cm rods, calibrated with an acoustic Doppler velocimeter
dose: high epsilon ~10^-4 m2 s-3, low epsilon ~10^-8 m2 s-3, unstirred control; continuous mixing
duration: 1-2 weeks continuous mixing after a 1-day unmixed acclimation
result: High turbulence cut net growth of Ceratium fusus ~25-50% and drove C. tripos and Pyrocystis noctiluca to net mortality (growth <0); four species (A. catenella, A. tamarense, Gyrodinium sp., P. fusiformis) were essentially unaffected; A. fundyense, G. catenatum and L. polyedrum grew ~30-40% faster. Low turbulence (10^-8) had no significant effect on any species.
key_details: Ten dinoflagellate species (30-500 um) were grown in three 20 L tanks: high turbulence, low turbulence and an unstirred control, with treatments rotated among tanks. Most species were run in duplicate experiments (C. tripos in three, across two clones); cells were counted about every other day and net growth taken from log-linear regressions. Growth was inhibited in 3 species (C. fusus, C. tripos, P. noctiluca; the last two with net mortality), unchanged in 4 (A. catenella fell ~15% in one of two runs only) and raised ~30-40% in 3 (A. fundyense 0.38 to 0.53 and 0.37 to 0.50 div/d; L. polyedrum 0.33 to 0.53 and 0.33 to 0.49 div/d; G. catenatum significant in one of two runs). L. polyedrum cells were smaller under high turbulence. Caveat: the HAB taxa most relevant to mitigation (Alexandrium, Lingulodinium, Gymnodinium catenatum) grew faster or were unaffected.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record says 1 species slower and 2 'no increase'; the full text reports 3 species inhibited (C. fusus slower; C. tripos and P. noctiluca net mortality under high turbulence), 4 unaffected and 3 faster.

title: Effect of growth conditions on flow‐induced inhibition of population growth of a red‐tide dinoflagellate
scale: Couette + shaken flasks
dose: τ = 0.004 Pa, 1 h/day
result: Growth cut was larger when flow was given in the last hour of dark, under low light, and in late-exponential cultures.

title: MECHANISMS OF FLUID SHEAR‐INDUCED INHIBITION OF POPULATION GROWTH IN A RED‐TIDE DINOFLAGELLATE 1
scale: isolated cells in 0.5 mL multiwell plates (shaken) and larger cultures in Couette-flow chambers and shaken flasks
dose: Couette laminar shear 0.004, 0.010 or 0.019 N m-2 for 1 to 24 h/day; unquantified shaking
result: At 0.004 N m-2, 1 h/day cut net growth 25.9 +/- 3.9% and 2-24 h/day ~50% (49.9 +/- 3.0%), entirely through fewer divisions; at 0.010-0.019 N m-2, 1 h/day cut growth 44.8 +/- 4.4% and continuous 0.019 N m-2 61.9 +/- 8.2%, with added mortality; shaken flasks gave 66.5 +/- 2.9%.
key_details: Lingulodinium polyedrum was tested three ways: shaken isolated cells tracked individually, Couette chambers at quantified shear, and shaken flasks; division frequency came from flow-cytometric DNA per cell. In isolated cells, percent dividing fell with daily shaking duration (F3,12 = 16.38, P = 0.0002) while mortality was unrelated to shaking. At the lowest shear, growth loss matched lower division; at higher shear and in shaken flasks, net growth fell below division estimates, showing shear-induced mortality. In a late-exponential culture at 0.004 N m-2 continuous, 23.6% of cells were disrupted (dead) vs 0.4% in controls. Caveat: statistics used within-experiment replicates, not replicated treatments, and a single shaker table was used for the isolated-cell tests.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record's 'Duration: Not reported' can be filled: shear was applied 1-24 h/day over multi-day runs. Growth-inhibition magnitudes (26-67%) were missing from the record.

title: Effect of fully characterized unsteady flow on population growth of the dinoflagellate Lingulodinium polyedrum
scale: Couette flow chambers, 170 mL culture each; 12 chambers per paired experiment (4 still controls + 4 per flow treatment)
dose: Steady shear 1.8-8 s⁻¹ vs oscillatory (unsteady) flow, average absolute shear 1.8-4 s⁻¹ (max 6.4-6.7 s⁻¹), periods 60-600 s
duration: Daily flow exposure 5 min to 2 h (standard 2 h/d, starting 2 h before end of night phase), over multi-day growth experiments
result: At average absolute shear 4 s⁻¹ for 2 h/d, unsteady flow gave 93.5% ± 35.4% growth inhibition vs 46.5% ± 26.7% for steady flow (p = 0.014); at 1.8 s⁻¹ the two were similar (45% vs 43%). Even 5 min/d of unsteady flow gave 11% inhibition, rising with duration.
key_details: Lab study of one L. polyedrum strain in oscillatory Couette chambers with analytically characterised shear. Paired design: each experiment had 4 still controls run simultaneously with two flow treatments of 4 chambers; still-control net growth was 0.14 ± 0.03 d⁻¹ (n = 57 chambers). Unsteady flow at 4 s⁻¹ average absolute shear nearly stopped net growth (93.5% inhibition over periods 60-300 s), 50% more than steady 4 s⁻¹, and was not different from steady 8 s⁻¹. Oscillation period (60-600 s) and flow-direction reversal did not matter; inhibition rose with daily exposure from 11% at 5 min. Effect is growth inhibition (not cell kill) and the difference between steady and unsteady shrank at lower shear.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record gives 'mean |γ| 4 s⁻¹' but omits the headline numbers (93.5% vs 46.5% inhibition) and that the unsteady-vs-steady difference vanishes at 1.8 s⁻¹. Duration '5-120 min' is daily exposure, not total experiment length.

title: Net growth of the bloom-forming dinoflagellate Heterocapsa triquetra and pH: why turbulence matters
scale: Eight 2 L Plexiglas containers with oscillating grids (4 replicates per level in Expt 1)
dose: Four turbulence levels, ε = 0.0001, 0.005, 0.05 and 1 cm² s⁻³ (10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁴ m² s⁻³)
result: Net growth was ~0.42 d⁻¹ at all turbulence levels while pH < 8.9; once densities exceeded 3 × 10⁴ cells/mL, growth was 0.17 d⁻¹ at the highest turbulence vs 0.07 d⁻¹ at the lowest (p = 0.006), because turbulence lowered pH via CO2 exchange. Turbulence did not suppress this dinoflagellate.
env_effects: Turbulence relieves CO2 limitation and holds pH down, which can help algae.
key_details: Lab batch cultures of Heterocapsa triquetra (clone K-0481) in f/2 at 15°C, grids at 4 turbulence levels spanning calm to storm conditions, 10 d. Expt 1 compared T1 vs T4 (4 replicates); Expt 2 compared T1-T3. No growth difference among levels for Days 0-5 (p = 0.914 and 0.909). At high density, T4 (0.17 d⁻¹) and T3 (0.13 d⁻¹) grew faster than T1/T2 (0.07 d⁻¹); pH was lower at high turbulence (p = 0.041). Cell volume (~3000 µm³) unaffected. Turbulence helped rather than hindered the bloom-former at high pH.

title: Role of turbulence in Dinophysis spp. growth, feeding, and toxin leakage in culture
organism: Dinophysis acuminata, D. ovum, D. caudata
scale: lab cultures
result: Slower growth in 2 species, faster in D. caudata.
env_effects: More intracellular toxin (D. acuminata) and toxin leakage (D. ovum).

title: Effects of turbulence on plankton: an overview of experimental evidence and some theoretical considerations
scale: review of lab data
dose: many
result: In a meta-analysis of normalized rates, growth was generally reduced by turbulence; dinoflagellates showed the strongest response (rate_x = -0.91 - 0.31 log ε, R = 0.55; bulk 121% decrease in normalized growth rate) and made up 53% of negative-effect cases.
key_details: Review and re-analysis of published lab data on small-scale turbulence effects on plankton growth, ingestion and energy expenditure, normalized as rate_x. Dinoflagellates (20-200 µm) showed the clearest negative growth response, with a bulk 121% decrease in normalized growth rate. Without dinoflagellates the growth-rate cloud was slightly positive and not distinguishable from 0. Ingestion rates mostly increased, especially below 10 cm² s⁻³. Many experiments used ε far above oceanic levels.

title: Combined effects of nutrients and small-scale turbulence in a microcosm experiment. I. Dynamics and size distribution of osmotrophic plankton
organism: Natural NW Mediterranean coastal plankton (phytoplankton and bacteria), <150 µm
scale: Twelve 15 L microcosms (6 turbulent, 6 still), 2 replicates per nutrient treatment (control, N-surplus N:P 160, Redfield N:P 16)
dose: Oscillating grids, ε = 0.055 cm² s⁻³ (5.5 × 10⁻⁶ m² s⁻³)
result: With nutrients added, turbulence raised total chl a (turbulent NP peaked at 19.0 ± 1.1 µg/L vs still maximum 4.2 ± 0.2 µg/L) and the >10 µm (diatom) fraction; without nutrients turbulence had no effect. Turbulence increased, not reduced, phytoplankton.
key_details: Coastal water from Masnou (Catalan coast) enclosed March 1998 in 15 L microcosms at 15°C for 8 d. Design: 3 nutrient conditions x still/turbulent, 2 replicate microcosms each (no replicates for TN and TNP on Day 8). In N and NP treatments turbulent chl a was significantly higher than still from Day 2 (p < 0.001); turbulent N reached 10.2 µg/L, still N peaked at 3.7 ± 2.5 µg/L. Bacterial abundance did not differ between still and turbulent. Turbulence shifted the community to larger cells and diatoms; small replication (n = 2).
fulltext_discrepancy: Record does not state that turbulence roughly quadrupled chlorophyll in nutrient-enriched microcosms (i.e. mixing enhanced growth).

title: Effects of small-scale turbulence on the growth of two diatoms of different size in a phosphorus-limited medium
scale: 2.5 L polycarbonate bottles, 2 still and 2 turbulent per species (n=2), two independent experiments
dose: orbital shaker at 130 rpm; epsilon ~10 cm2 s-3 (ADV-estimated) vs still
result: Turbulence raised Coscinodiscus growth (0.37 to 0.42 and 0.27 to 0.32 d-1; final 33 vs 55 and 22 vs 38 cells/mL) and slightly lowered T. pseudonana growth (1.74 to 1.52 and 1.69 to 1.35 d-1).
key_details: Batch cultures of the small diatom Thalassiosira pseudonana (~6 um) and the large Coscinodiscus sp. (~109 um) were grown in P-limited medium (1 uM P, N/P 88.2) at 22 C with duplicate still and turbulent bottles, in two experiments. Turbulence increased Coscinodiscus growth rate and final density in both experiments and slightly reduced T. pseudonana growth. Results were compared with a nutrient-uptake (Sherwood number) model; Sh under turbulence was 1.17 for T. pseudonana and 2.94 for Coscinodiscus. Caveats: n=2 bottles per treatment, non-axenic cultures, Coscinodiscus growth computed from total shells including empty ones.

title: The effects of turbulence on the growth of three different diatom species
organism: Thalassiosira pseudonana, Skeletonema costatum, Phaeodactylum tricornutum
scale: orbital shaker 0-180 rpm
result: T. pseudonana final density 33.5 → 46-58 × 10⁵ mL⁻¹ (up); Skeletonema up but inhibited at 180 rpm after day 7; Phaeodactylum ~no difference.

title: Effects of agitation on the microalgae Phaeodactylum tricornutum and Porphyridium cruentum
scale: 5 L baffled stirred-tank photobioreactor (BioFlo III), continuous culture at dilution rate 0.0139 h-1, aerated 1.5 L/min
dose: stepwise impeller speed 150-550 rpm (P. tricornutum; tip speed 0.68 to >1.56 m/s) and up to 650 rpm (P. cruentum); Pluronic F68 0.01-0.10% w/v
result: Steady-state biomass rose with agitation up to 350 rpm (1.56 m/s tip speed) for P. tricornutum and 550 rpm (2.45 m/s) for P. cruentum, then fell; P. cruentum washed out at 650 rpm. Damage came from small bubbles rupturing at the surface, and Pluronic F68 protected cells in a dose-dependent way.
key_details: Continuous monocultures of Phaeodactylum tricornutum and Porphyridium cruentum were run in a 5 L stirred photobioreactor with agitation raised stepwise; damage was inferred from falls in steady-state biomass at constant dilution rate. pH was held at 7.7 by CO2 injection, and kLa rose with agitation, so CO2 limitation did not explain the decline. Below the threshold, more agitation raised biomass through better light-dark cycling. The authors note that the net biomass data cannot separate growth and death effects, so relative shear sensitivity of the two species is not firmly established. This is a bioprocess study, not HAB control.
fulltext_discrepancy: The P. cruentum damage threshold (between 2.45 and 2.89 m/s tip speed) was missing from the record, and agitation below the threshold increased biomass.

title: Hydrodynamic stress and lethal events in sparged microalgae cultures
organism: Dunaliella tertiolecta, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii wild type and cell-wall-lacking mutant (non-HAB production strains)
scale: Lab bubble columns (continuous and batch) plus a pilot-plant bubble column
dose: superficial gas velocity up to 0.085 m/s
result: No cell damage in D. tertiolecta or wild-type C. reinhardtii up to superficial gas velocities of 0.076 and 0.085 m/s; the wall-less mutant died at 0.46 ± 0.08 h⁻¹ (0.076 m/s) and 1.01 ± 0.29 h⁻¹ (0.085 m/s). Varying sparger nozzles gave D. tertiolecta death of 0.047 ± 0.016 h⁻¹ at high gas entrance velocity, implicating the sparger rather than bubble bursting.
env_effects: Rising bubbles harmless to walled cells.
key_details: Photobioreactor engineering study, not a bloom-control test. Superficial gas velocity alone did not kill walled cells; the cell wall protected against hydrodynamic shear. In a pilot-plant column at up to 0.026 m/s with low gas entrance velocities, D. tertiolecta showed no damage. Authors conclude gas entrance velocity at the sparger is the likely main cause of cell death. Relevance to HAB mitigation is indirect: bubbling is unlikely to kill walled algae except at the nozzle.

title: The Sensitivity of the Dinoflagellate Crypthecodinium cohnii to Transient Hydrodynamic Forces and Cell‐Bubble Interactions
scale: microfluidic contraction + bubbles
dose: microfluidic flow contraction at 10-90 mL/min (weighted EDR up to ~5.8 x 10^7 W/m3), 1-3 passes; bubbles from a 30-gauge needle (~5 mm) or sintered-glass sparger (~1 mm)
duration: single transient passes (1-3) through the contraction device
result: No lysis (LDH and counts) at any flow up to 5.8 x 10^7 W/m3, but motility fell from 87% to 24% after one pass and 2% after three at 90 mL/min from loss of the longitudinal flagellum, which regrew during static recovery. Small bubbles cut motility (~20% loss vs ~4% for large bubbles) and enriched cells in foam up to 1.80x.
key_details: Crypthecodinium cohnii (a heterotrophic DHA-producing dinoflagellate) at 3.5 x 10^6 cells/mL was pumped through a microfluidic contraction whose energy dissipation rate was estimated by CFD. Lysis was measured by LDH release and cell counts; none was significant. Motility after 1, 2 and 3 passes at 90 mL/min was 24, 6 and 2% vs 87% initially; at 50 mL/min it was 70, 67 and 62%. Cells attached to bubble films and were trapped in foam Plateau borders; Pluronic F-68 reduced film attachment but not trapping. Caveat: bioprocess study on a non-HAB species; effects are sublethal and reversible.
fulltext_discrepancy: Flagellar loss and motility decline were reversible (flagella regrew during static recovery), a detail missing from the record.

title: Effects of shear stress on the microalgae Chaetoceros muelleri
scale: Couette shear cylinders (rheometer-calibrated), laminar flow, medium thickened with locust bean gum (0, 0.3, 0.5%)
dose: 0-500 rpm (shear rate up to 1,079 s⁻¹; shear stress up to 19.4 Pa)
duration: 1 h exposure at 4 °C; time series 1-120 min at 100 rpm
result: Viability threshold τ = 1-1.3 Pa, above which viability drops to 52-66%; effect within 1 min.
key_details: Early-stationary C. muelleri was sheared in Couette cylinders, with viscosity raised by locust bean gum so flow stayed laminar. Viability was scored by FDA staining, and all exposures were run in triplicate. Shear stress up to 1 Pa had no effect; above 1.3 Pa viability dropped sharply to 52-66%. Most of the effect happened within 1 min, with a secondary effect up to 8 min. This is a bioreactor-engineering study, not a bloom-control test.

title: Controlling spring Dinoflagellate blooms in a stratified drinking water reservoir via artificial mixing: Effects, mechanisms, and operational thresholds
organism: spring dinoflagellate bloom dominated by Peridiniopsis sp. (also Chlorophyta e.g. Closterium, Bacillariophyta e.g. Cyclotella)
scale: Lijiahe Reservoir, Xi'an, China (2.18 km2, max depth 80 m, 5.7 x 10^7 m3); eight water-lifting aerators installed 2007; sampled at 2 sites
dose: 8 water-lifting aerators (diffusers 5 m above sediment; aeration <20 m3/h, lifting flow 20-50 m3/h each)
duration: 2 weeks of operation (April 9-22, 2021); monitoring March 6 - May 5, 2021
result: Within two weeks of mixing, surface dinoflagellate density fell 97.8% (S1) and 96.8% (S2) from pre-mixing peaks of 2.2 x 10^7 and 1.1 x 10^7 cells/L to <5.0 x 10^5 cells/L; total phytoplankton fell 97.1% and 95.5%, and Chl-a stayed <10 ug/L.
env_effects: Community shifted from large motile taxa (dinoflagellates, Closterium) to small non-motile diatoms (Cyclotella, reduced only 70.0-84.0%); surface water temperature fell below 10 C and stratification weakened (dT 6.8 to 2.3 C at S1).
key_details: Before-during-after field study of one spring bloom (2021) in a eutrophic, stratified drinking-water reservoir: 8 water-lifting aerators ran for two weeks at bloom onset, with weekly to twice-weekly profiles at two sites near the aerators. Pre-mixing surface peaks reached 2.4 x 10^7 cells/L total phytoplankton (Chl-a 438.8 ug/L) at S1. Reductions compare surface densities during mixing with the pre-mixing surface peak, so part of the drop is vertical redistribution (dilution through the water column), which the authors note alongside cell decay. RDA identified water temperature, Zmix, Zeu/Zmix and TP as the main drivers (69.9% of variance for taxonomic groups). Caveats: no unmixed control site or year, a single event, and the two sites were both inside the aerator zone.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record's -95.5 to -97.1% are total phytoplankton surface reductions; dinoflagellates specifically fell 96.8-97.8%. The record's effect_pct 95.5 is the total-phytoplankton figure at S2.

title: Artificial mixing to control cyanobacterial blooms: a review
scale: lakes and reservoirs
dose: bubble plumes
result: Table 1 lists 13 lake/reservoir mixing applications: reduced cyanobacteria in several (e.g. Lake Brooker, Solomon Dam, Nieuwe Meer, Dalbang, Bleiloch), no effect in others (East Sidney, Chaffey, Sheldon; Lake Yogo 0/?; North Pine -/0). Mixing shifts dominance to greens and diatoms when it is deep and entrains cells, but chl-a per m² often rises.
key_details: Narrative review of artificial mixing (mostly aeration/bubble plumes) aimed at cyanobacteria. The authors tabulate 13 lake/reservoir applications (Table 1). Mixing lowered surface temperature (e.g. Nieuwe Meer 23.4 → 19.1 °C), raised hypolimnetic O2 and often lowered surface pH by 0.5-1 unit. Chaffey Reservoir SRP release from sediment fell ~80%, but Gächter and Wehrli found 10 years of mixing did not stop sediment anoxia or internal P cycling. Standing crop (chl-a per m²) often increased as nutrients were entrained. The authors conclude mixing can shift composition away from cyanobacteria but external nutrient reduction should stay the main focus.

title: Effect of Artificial Circulation on the Removal Kinetics of Cyanobacteria in a Hypereutrophic Shallow Lake
scale: Santo Anastácio Lake, Fortaleza, Brazil (tropical, ~0.3 hm³, max depth 3.8 m, hypereutrophic); single point-source bubble diffuser at 1.5 m depth, samples inside plume (x = 0) vs outside (x = 2 m)
dose: Air flow rates Q = 1.9, 3.8, 5.7 and 7.6 NL/s (7.5 kW compressor; diffuser with 160 × 1 mm holes)
duration: 120 min per aeration test (November 2014; pre-aeration survey November 2013)
result: After each 120-min test, depth-averaged chl-a was 5-20% lower inside the bubble plume than outside, the gap growing with air flow; first-order net reduction rates scaled with plume hydrodynamics/ε and tracked pheophytin-a production, indicating cell death.
key_details: Field test in a shallow hypereutrophic Brazilian lake: a pre-aeration survey (Nov 2013) characterised natural variability, then four aeration tests at different air flows (Nov 2014), with repeat tests at 3.8 and 5.7 NL/s on 11 Nov 2014. Samples every 5-30 min at several depths and distances; the 'control' is water 2 m from the plume, where plume velocity was negligible (no separate control lake). In one test chl-a rose both inside and outside the plume (slower inside); in the other three it fell in both, faster inside. First-order fits had r > 0.97. Local, short-term effect only; whole-lake effect is extrapolated by simulation, not measured.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record lacks the magnitude (chl-a 5-20% lower inside vs outside plume after 120 min), the air flow rates (1.9-7.6 NL/s) and duration (120-min tests); the effect is local to the plume, not lake-wide.

title: Effectiveness of ozone nanobubble treatments on high biomass cyanobacterial blooms: A mesocosm experiment and field trial
scale: 2,000 L mesocosm + embayment
dose: O2 nanobubbles vs ozone nanobubbles
result: Ozone nanobubbles -98-99% chl-a; oxygen-only nanobubbles had no effect; embayment trial no effect.

title: Artificially generated turbulence: a review of phycological nanocosm, microcosm, and mesocosm experiments
scale: Review of 102 publications on lab turbulence cosms (grid 32, shaker 19, Couette 18, aeration 11, other 21 studies)
dose: n/a
result: Report ε; most lab cosms are too small for large eddies; acrylic can leach toxins under UV.
key_details: Methods review of how lab studies generate and quantify turbulence for phytoplankton (102 publications). Grid-generated turbulence dominates (32 studies, 29 quantified). Couette cylinders (18) are usually quantified as shear rate, not ε. Shaker tables (19) and aeration (11) are often unquantified. Most cosms hold <1 m³, which limits the largest eddies. Dinoflagellates were the most studied group because of their HAB relevance. Read from the authors' accepted manuscript.
